value.overview: The Streak-breasted Treehunter is a large, secretive furnariid of the humid mountains of Costa Rica and western Panama. It usually remains in dense, mossy forest understory, where its brown plumage provides excellent camouflage. Despite its name, it is more often seen clambering through tangled vegetation, epiphytes, and fallen leaves than high in the tree canopy. It is an uncommon but locally regular resident of suitable montane habitat.
value.classification: The Streak-breasted Treehunter belongs to the ovenbird family Furnariidae and the foliage-gleaner subfamily Furnariinae. It is the only recognized species in its genus, Thripadectes, and is currently treated as monotypic.
value.identification: This is a fairly large, heavy-bodied brown bird with a strong, slightly curved bill and a long chestnut-brown tail. The upperparts are dark brown, with a darker crown and subtle olive streaking. The throat and upper breast are ochraceous to brown and marked with narrow dark streaks, while the lower underparts are less strongly patterned. The sexes look alike. Its furtive movements in dense vegetation and scratchy, rolling calls are useful clues to identification.
value.rangeHabitat: The species has a restricted Central American range, occurring from the highlands of Costa Rica into western Panama as far east as Veraguas. In Costa Rica it is found through much of the Talamancan mountain region, including suitable sites in the Central and southern highlands. It occupies humid montane evergreen forest, especially shady ravines near streams with abundant mosses, epiphytes, tangled undergrowth, and fallen debris. It may also use mature secondary forest adjoining intact habitat, generally from about 700 to 2,500 meters.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and throughout its small range; it is not known to undertake regular seasonal migration. Individuals may move locally with changing conditions, but Costa Rican records represent year-round occurrence rather than a passage population.
value.breeding: Breeding has been reported mainly from February through August. The nest is placed at the end of a tunnel excavated into an earthen bank, often in a steep or shaded part of the forest. The tunnel may extend roughly 60 to 70 centimeters and leads to a chamber lined with leaf stems, rootlets, or similar plant material. The usual clutch is two eggs. Both parents feed the young, and males have been observed incubating.
value.dietFeeding: The Streak-breasted Treehunter feeds mainly on arthropods, including insects and spiders, and also takes small vertebrates such as frogs, salamanders, and occasionally lizards. It searches dense understory, mossy branches, epiphytes, dead leaves, and accumulations of forest debris. The bird may tear apart leaf clusters to expose prey and sometimes hangs upside down while foraging. It is usually solitary or found in pairs and only rarely joins mixed-species feeding flocks.
value.behavior: This species is generally quiet and difficult to see because it moves through dense, shaded vegetation close to the ground or in the lower understory. It hops and clambers along branches, vines, banks, and tangled debris while probing and tearing at vegetation. It is normally encountered alone, though pairs may occur. Its calls include harsh, grating notes and rough, rolling phrases that can reveal its presence before the bird becomes visible.

conservation.populationTrend: The population is considered stable, although the species is generally uncommon and locally distributed.
